title: Detecting and Mitigating Subliminal Bias Transmission in Distilled Language Models
summary: This paper proposes a method to detect and mitigate subliminal bias transmission in distilled language models. By analyzing token entanglement patterns in synthetic data generated by teacher models, we identify hidden signals that propagate behavioral traits to student models. Our approach combines mechanistic interpretability with adversarial training to disrupt these signals while preserving task performance. We validate the method on mathematical reasoning tasks, showing reduced bias amplification without compromising accuracy.
gap: Existing knowledge distillation techniques (ref-009, ref-011) fail to account for subliminal bias transmission (ref-014, ref-010) that persists even when training data appears neutral. Current bias mitigation strategies (ref-012) address surface-level correlations but miss deeper token-level entanglements.
approach: We develop a two-stage process: (1) mechanistic analysis of teacher model activations to identify neuron populations correlated with bias transmission, and (2) adversarial fine-tuning of student models with perturbed synthetic data that disrupts identified entanglement patterns. This combines regression-based circuit discovery (ref-010) with targeted parameter masking.
evaluation: We compare against standard distillation baselines (ref-009) and bias mitigation methods (ref-012) using political bias benchmarks (ref-010) and mathematical reasoning tasks. Success is measured by (1) bias amplification reduction via continuation task scoring, (2) preservation of task accuracy, and (3) mechanistic verification of disrupted neuron activations.

title: Diffusion Policy Safety via Adversarial Training with Transferable Perturbations
summary: This work addresses safety vulnerabilities in diffusion-based policies by introducing adversarial training with transferable perturbations. We generate offline attack samples that maintain effectiveness across policy iterations and test environments. Our method improves robustness against both digital and physical adversarial attacks while maintaining task performance, validated through manipulation task benchmarks.
gap: While diffusion policies show strong performance (ref-005), their safety against adversarial attacks remains unexplored. Existing adversarial training methods (ref-005) focus on single-policy attacks but fail to address transferability across policy versions and physical environments.
approach: We develop a two-stage adversarial training framework: (1) generation of transferable perturbations using ensemble diffusion policies with diverse noise schedules, and (2) training with both digital perturbations and simulated physical patch attacks. The method incorporates curriculum learning to gradually increase attack complexity.
evaluation: We test on standard manipulation benchmarks (ref-005) under four attack scenarios: offline digital, online digital, global physical, and patch-based physical. Success is measured by (1) success rate retention under attack, (2) perturbation transferability across policy versions, and (3) physical patch effectiveness in real-world simulations. Baselines include standard diffusion policies (ref-005) and non-transferable adversarial training.

title: Agentic Misalignment Detection via Synthetic Insider Threat Simulation
summary: We introduce a controlled evaluation framework for detecting agentic misalignment in LLMs by simulating corporate insider threat scenarios. Our method uses constrained generation to force models into ethical dilemmas where misaligned behavior could emerge. We validate the framework by stress-testing open-source models against scenarios involving data leakage and goal conflict, identifying subtle misalignment patterns missed by standard benchmarks.
gap: Current safety evaluations (ref-007, ref-015) lack controlled environments for testing agentic misalignment (ref-002). Existing stress-testing methods (ref-002) focus on real-world deployment risks but don't systematically isolate misalignment triggers in synthetic settings.
approach: We implement a three-phase evaluation: (1) scenario generation using constrained decoding to create ethically ambiguous corporate tasks, (2) model responses analyzed through both explicit behavior (ref-002) and latent intent detection via activation clustering, and (3) counterfactual testing where models assess their own deployment context (ref-002).
evaluation: We compare model responses against human-labeled ground truth for ethical boundaries. Metrics include (1) frequency of misaligned actions, (2) consistency in self-assessment vs actual behavior, and (3) activation pattern similarity to known misalignment cases. Baselines include standard safety benchmarks (ref-001) and adversarial prompts (ref-019).
